documents.unit: UK ADVANCE (Office of the Provost generative AI committee)
documents.title: UK ADVANCE 2025 Guidelines and Recommendations for Generative AI in Instructional Contexts
documents.summary: University-wide guidelines from the provost's UK ADVANCE committee on AI risks, how instructors write and communicate course policies, how to respond to suspected misuse, and how to design assignments. It lays out a four-area policy spectrum, expects documentation of AI use where allowed, and recommends against AI detectors, leaving the stance to instructors.
documents.stance_why: The document sets no university-wide ban or permission. It says 'While instructors will adopt a range of policies and approaches' and that policies 'will fall within one of four areas on a spectrum: No use, Use only when/as directed, Use freely in certain cases, Use freely in all cases', so it hands the decision to instructors and lists tiers.

units.why: The footnote defines 'generative AI' ('any platform, software, model, tool, function or feature that generates novel text or other media output') to set what the guidelines cover, so P61, informs, general.
units.anchor: refer to any platform, software, model, tool, function or feature that generates novel text or

units.why: The footnote says the guidelines cover AI built into everyday software ('Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Adobe Creative Suite, Zoom, Blackboard, Canvas'). Nearest type is P07 (embedded AI), though these are office and LMS tools, not IDEs.
units.anchor: increasingly being integrated into existing software and platforms such as Microsoft 365
units.policy: Generative AI tools and functions are increasingly being integrated into existing software and platforms such as Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Adobe Creative Suite, Zoom, Blackboard, Canvas and Apple iOS.
units.fit_note: Covers AI embedded in office, video and LMS platforms, not editors/IDEs or coding agents.

units.why: The Executive Summary says the guidelines 'may be updated to reflect the nature of the field as it continues to change', i.e. provisional policy: P54, informs.
units.anchor: may be updated to reflect the nature of the field as it continues to change

units.why: Describes how the university 'empaneled UK ADVANCE, a transdisciplinary committee of experts' in June 2023, i.e. who made the guidelines and how: P84, informs.
units.anchor: empaneled UK ADVANCE, a transdisciplinary committee of experts

units.why: Says UK ADVANCE takes 'an evidence-based approach' with 'ongoing monitoring of experiences among our campus, community and nationally', which is gathering evidence on AI in education: P55, informs.
units.anchor: evidence-based approach with experts across the disciplines and ongoing monitoring of experiences

units.why: The summary lists what the guidelines cover (understanding risks, course policies, misuse response, assignment design); it states purpose and scope of an institution-level framework: P56, informs.
units.anchor: understanding capabilities and risks of generative AI for education
units.policy: UK ADVANCE offers guidance and recommendations for understanding capabilities and risks of generative AI for education, developing and communicating course policies on generative AI, responding to possible misuse in coursework, and designing assignments, curricula and learning experiences.

units.why: Says an understanding of AI capabilities and risks 'is foundational' for AI literacy 'essential for both instructor and student success'. It frames AI literacy as a needed skill; nearest is P44, but no employer or career claim is made.
units.anchor: an understanding of the capabilities and risks of AI is foundational
units.fit_note: Frames AI literacy as essential for instructors and students; does not mention employers or careers.

units.why: The Recommendation says 'instructors and students should consider the following when using any generative AI tool' (privacy, accuracy, learning, ethics): a general responsible-use principle, P56, should.
units.anchor: instructors and students should consider the following when using any generative AI tool

units.why: 'Student education records (as defined by FERPA) and protected research data should not be provided to generative AI tools unless/until they have been vetted' and approved: protects confidential data and requires vetted tools, P50, should-not.
units.anchor: should not be provided to generative AI tools unless/until they have been vetted for data
units.policy: Student education records (as defined by FERPA) and protected research data should not be provided to generative AI tools unless or until they have been vetted for data privacy and other governance issues and approved by the University for the proposed use.

units.why: Advises it is 'important to review any terms of use and privacy policies before registering a user account with any AI service', a data-protection precaution: P50, should.
units.anchor: terms of use and privacy policies before registering a user account with any AI service

units.why: Says awareness of third-party information sharing 'becomes central to data privacy and digital hygiene' as AI integrates with other software; a privacy principle: P50, informs.
units.anchor: becomes central to data privacy and digital hygiene

units.why: Reports that UK faculty and staff 'can purchase individual licenses to Microsoft Copilot' that is 'compliant with FERPA and research integrity requirements'. An institution-wide licensed tool (P92, not course-specific P17), may.
units.anchor: can purchase individual licenses to Microsoft Copilot

units.why: Says open-source models 'may be installed on protected servers, but these should also be carefully reviewed for privacy and governance issues': a vetting condition on tools, P65, should.
units.anchor: should also be carefully reviewed for privacy and governance issues
units.fit_note: Individuals review open-source models they install; not an institutional approval process.

units.why: Warns AI tools 'may produce hallucinations or confabulations' and that 'verification and evaluation of the output will be a critical component of informed use': P31, should.
units.anchor: verification and evaluation of the output will be a critical component of informed use

units.why: Observes 'an overreliance on AI tools may bypass opportunities for meaningful learning and the development of students' skills and agency': AI can shortcut skill-building practice, P41, informs.
units.anchor: overreliance on AI tools may bypass opportunities for meaningful learning

units.why: Lists benefits of AI ('coaching or tutoring, facilitating personalized learning, simulating interactions... analyzing data') without a rule or a career claim: P87, informs.
units.anchor: Generative AI offers a growing range of possibilities to enhance institutional and instructor efficacy

units.why: States effective AI use 'relies on active engagement, reflective and self-regulated learning, transparency and accountability'. A principle that keeps students actively engaged, nearest P32.
units.anchor: consistently relies on active engagement, reflective and self-regulated learning, transparency and accountability
units.fit_note: Names engagement, self-regulation and transparency as conditions of effective use, not only that the student stays the primary thinker.

units.why: 'Instructors are encouraged to have open conversations with students about appropriate and effective use of AI' means discussing AI rules with students: P66, should.
units.anchor: Instructors are encouraged to have open conversations with students about appropriate and effective use of

units.why: Raises ethics concerns including biases models 'might inherit and propagate from the datasets' and 'impact on the environment': P53, informs. IP appears in the same sentence but the framing is ethics and bias.
units.anchor: any biases that the models might inherit and propagate from the datasets
units.fit_note: Also raises intellectual property of training data and output (P52).

units.why: Notes 'there may also be cost barriers to accessing features, capabilities and allowances in more powerful models and subscription-based accounts': equity and access, P51, informs.
units.anchor: there may also be cost barriers to accessing features, capabilities and allowances

units.why: Says before downloading an open-source model 'instructors should assess possible risks and consult with UK Information Technology Services': a review step before using a tool, P65, should.
units.anchor: instructors should assess possible risks and consult with UK Information Technology Services
units.fit_note: Individual instructors consult IT before using a tool; not an institutional approval process.

units.why: Says any use of AI, open-source or proprietary, 'requires attention to accuracy, agency, ethics, bias and impact of use': a general responsible-use caution, P56, informs.
units.anchor: requires attention to accuracy, agency, ethics, bias and impact of use

units.why: States 'clarity around expectations for student use of generative AI is essential' because students navigate different policies across courses; it explains why expectations must be communicated (P66, a reason, rather than P09, a requirement).
units.anchor: Clarity around expectations for student use of generative AI is essential for student success
units.fit_note: Gives the reason expectations must be clear (students navigate many different policies).

units.why: Notes students 'may even be reluctant to ask about expectations in the face of ambiguity'; it is a reason to be explicit, not an instruction to ask (so not P10): P66, informs.
units.anchor: reluctant to ask about expectations in the face of ambiguity
units.fit_note: Observes students are reluctant to ask; does not tell students to ask (P10).

units.why: Says expectations 'should be made clear for students both verbally and on syllabi and other locations... (e.g., Canvas)': communicating AI policy in syllabus and course sites, P09, should.
units.anchor: they should be made clear for students both verbally and on syllabi

units.why: Points to CELT's 'range of example AI course policies using different rationales for instructors to adapt'; a resource for faculty setting policy, P63, informs.
units.anchor: maintains a range of example AI course policies using different rationales for instructors to adapt
units.fit_note: Provides example course policies for adaptation, not workshops or consultation alone.

units.why: 'We recommend that course policies exhibit four key characteristics' (people-centered, adaptability, effectiveness, awareness) are design principles for course policies: P56, should.
units.anchor: We recommend that course policies exhibit four key characteristics
units.fit_note: Principles for writing course-level policies rather than an institution-wide rule.

units.why: Says generative AI should be used 'to augment, rather than replace, instructor decision-making and student learning': humans stay in control and students keep thinking, P32, should.
units.anchor: used to augment — rather than replace — instructor decision-making and student learning

units.why: Quotes the 'humans in the loop' idea: 'the human is fully aware and fully in control'. A human-oversight principle (P32 rather than P73, which is about decisions on people): informs.
units.anchor: the human is fully aware and fully in control

units.why: Says policies 'are best adapted to the local context of the course', including learning goals and instructor expertise: the rule follows learning goals (P83), should.
units.anchor: best adapted to the local context of the course
units.fit_note: Also says policies reflect the instructor's expertise and perspectives, so each instructor decides (P04).

units.why: States policies 'likely will fall within one of four areas on a spectrum': no use, use only when/as directed, use freely in certain cases, use freely in all cases: named tiers, P05.
units.anchor: one of four areas on a spectrum
units.policy: Instructors may adopt a range of course policies that likely fall within one of four areas on a spectrum: no use, use only when or as directed, use freely in certain cases, use freely in all cases.

units.why: For more restrictive policies an instructor 'may need to consider measures to ensure that the policy is followed', 'adapting assignments and holding certain activities during class meetings': assignment redesign, P35, may.
units.anchor: adapting assignments and holding certain activities during class meetings
units.fit_note: Also moves activities into class meetings (P33).

units.why: For restrictive policies 'it is important to understand the limitations of AI detectors': a caution about detectors, P39, informs.
units.anchor: it is important to understand the limitations of AI detectors

units.why: For permissive policies instructors 'may need to consider measures to ensure transparency and appropriate documentation of the use of generative AI': a disclosure measure, P24, may.
units.anchor: measures to ensure transparency and appropriate documentation of the use of generative AI
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors designing permissive policies, not directly to students.

units.why: 'Documentation of AI use may range from a brief statement to a detailed explanation... or links to... chatbot conversations' describes kinds of AI-use records: P26, informs.
units.anchor: may range from a brief statement to a detailed explanation of how AI tools were
units.fit_note: Describes a range of documentation, from brief statement to chat links; not a firm requirement.

units.why: 'Any questions or requests from students related to the use of generative AI as learning accommodations should be referred to the UK Disability Resource Center': routes accommodations, P97, should.
units.anchor: should be referred to the UK Disability Resource Center
units.fit_note: Referral rule for accommodation requests, not accessibility of tools or output.

units.why: An effective course policy includes 'a definition of generative AI', setting the policy's scope: P61, should.
units.anchor: A definition of generative AI
units.policy: An effective course policy includes a definition of generative AI, which may be expanded or revised to include information relevant to the course and discipline.

units.why: An effective policy includes 'a statement on whether the use of generative AI will be permitted for coursework and, if so, how and to what degree': an AI statement in the course policy, P09, should.
units.anchor: A statement on whether the use of generative AI will be permitted for coursework

units.why: An effective policy includes 'a specific description of what constitutes inappropriate use... as well as the consequences for inappropriate use': asks to state consequences in advance, P37, should.
units.anchor: what constitutes inappropriate use of generative AI in the course as well as the consequences
units.fit_note: Asks for a description of inappropriate use and consequences in general, not specific penalties.

units.why: An effective policy includes 'a process for students to document the use of generative AI for assignments and other course activities (if it is permitted)': a disclosure process, P24, should.
units.anchor: A process for students to document the use of generative AI for assignments
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors: the policy should provide a documentation process.

units.why: Says it 'is good practice to include the website or software that was used, the name of the AI model(s) and the date(s) of use': what an AI citation contains, P25, should.
units.anchor: good practice to include the website or software that was used, the name of the

units.why: An effective policy includes 'a rationale for the policy grounded in the context of the discipline or profession, the learning goals of the course... and/or ethics and academic integrity': explaining rules, P66, should.
units.anchor: A rationale for the policy grounded in the context of the discipline or profession

units.why: An effective policy includes 'links to resources for understanding and using generative AI ethically and effectively': course-level pointers to learning resources, P70, should.
units.anchor: Links to resources for understanding and using generative AI ethically and effectively
units.fit_note: Course-level links to AI literacy resources; not institutional training.

units.why: An effective policy has 'a learner-centered and student-friendly tone that builds understanding and motivation': wording the policy with care, P66, should.
units.anchor: A learner-centered and student-friendly tone that builds understanding and motivation

units.why: An effective policy includes 'an invitation for students to discuss any questions or concerns with the instructor': invites questions; nearest P10 but the instructor, not the student, is addressed.
units.anchor: An invitation for students to discuss any questions or concerns with the instructor
units.fit_note: Instructor invites questions; the type is about students asking before using AI.

units.why: Instructors can work with CELT for 'designing and communicating course policies'; CELT 'provides programs, workshops and resources on generative AI and consults with instructors': faculty support, P63, informs.
units.anchor: provides programs, workshops and resources on generative AI and consults with instructors

units.why: Lists a 'wider range of possible misuse of generative AI tools depending on the course policy', from copying text to 'asking generative AI tools for help' and 'revising or copyediting text'. It defines misuse as policy-dependent without declaring misconduct: P36, informs.
units.anchor: there is a wider range of possible misuse of generative AI tools depending on the
units.policy: There is a wider range of possible misuse of generative AI tools depending on the course policy, including copying text from generative AI, relying on its output as an initial draft, using its ideas, asking it for help, reusing its solutions, integrating small portions of its text, and revising or copyediting text with it.
units.fit_note: Lists a spectrum of possible misuse behaviors without declaring them misconduct.

units.why: 'Even if a student attributes their use of generative AI, it may still be misuse if course policy prohibits it': disclosure does not excuse prohibited use (P28), informs.
units.anchor: even if a student attributes their use of generative AI, it may still be

units.why: 'Clear policies will help students and instructors navigate the range of possible misuse cases and understand what to expect': a reason for clarity, P66, informs.
units.anchor: Clear policies will help students and instructors navigate the range of possible misuse cases

units.why: Cites Administrative Regulations 6.3.2, which 'defines plagiarism and cheating', and the Ombud's 'procedure for processing academic offenses'; AI misuse goes through existing integrity definitions and procedure: P81, informs.
units.anchor: defines plagiarism and cheating
units.policy: The UK Administrative Regulations 6.3.2 defines plagiarism and cheating, and the Ombud website provides information about the procedure for processing academic offenses.
units.fit_note: Cites the existing rules and procedure rather than stating steps.

units.why: Warns AI output 'may imitate or reproduce copyrighted material on which they were trained', a copyright concern: P52, informs.
units.anchor: may imitate or reproduce copyrighted material on which they were trained

units.why: Detectors 'can be prone to false positives'; relying on percentages 'may introduce bias... and demoralize students'. Detectors are unreliable: P39, informs.
units.anchor: They can be prone to false positives, i.e., indicating that all or part of a

units.why: Detectors 'can be evaded with a combination of prompt manipulation... and hand-editing the output': another reason detectors are unreliable, P39, informs.
units.anchor: They can be evaded with a combination of prompt manipulation

units.why: Detectors 'cannot be verified with matching sources (as opposed to similarity detectors...)': their output cannot be checked, P39, informs.
units.anchor: They cannot be verified with matching sources
units.fit_note: Contrasts detectors with similarity checkers that link to matching sources.

units.why: Detectors 'do not guarantee the protection, privacy and confidentiality' of what is input: a privacy risk and a reason against detectors, P50, informs.
units.anchor: do not guarantee the protection, privacy and confidentiality of any information, data or
units.fit_note: Used as a reason against detectors.

units.why: Detectors 'risk creating a surveillance-based or adversarial learning environment that can negatively affect student motivation, learning and belonging': a harm of detection, P53, informs.
units.anchor: risk creating a surveillance-based or adversarial learning environment
units.fit_note: Names a harm of detectors to belonging and motivation, not bias or environment.

units.why: 'Data on detectors will continue to emerge and require ongoing reassessment, which may result in updated guidelines': to be revisited, P54, informs.
units.anchor: require ongoing reassessment, which may result in updated guidelines

units.why: 'Student education records should not be input into third-party generative AI detection tools' until vetted and approved: a data-privacy prohibition, P50, should-not.
units.anchor: Student education records should not be input into third-party generative AI detection tools
units.policy: Student education records should not be input into third-party generative AI detection tools or systems unless and until the tools or systems have been vetted for data privacy and other AI governance issues and approved by the university for use.

units.why: 'We suggest consultation with the department chair or school director and the Academic Ombud' when misuse is suspected: a procedural step with officials, P81 rather than P57 (which is talking with the student), should.
units.anchor: we suggest consultation with the department chair or school director and the Academic Ombud
units.fit_note: Consultation with chair and Ombud before action; no filing deadline or form.

units.why: 'We recommend against the use of generative AI detectors for determining academic offenses': do not rely on detectors, P39, should-not.
units.anchor: we recommend against the use of generative AI detectors for determining academic offenses

units.why: UK ADVANCE 'will continue to monitor the landscape and update the guidelines as appropriate': a review commitment, P54, informs.
units.anchor: will continue to monitor the landscape and update the guidelines as appropriate

units.why: Assessments follow principles such as 'course and program learning outcomes' and 'authentic and engaging learning experiences' whether they 'seek to avoid the use of generative AI or engage students in it': assessment design, P35, informs.
units.anchor: Effective, learning-centered assessments follow from these principles whether they seek to avoid
units.fit_note: General assessment-design principles, not specific to AI changes.

units.why: Strategy: 'Segment larger assessments with checkpoints and/or multiple deliverables that value iterative processes along with final products'. Assignment redesign, P35, may.
units.anchor: Segment larger assessments with checkpoints and/or multiple deliverables

units.why: Strategy: 'Integrate work toward assessments into class meetings' so students study, draft and revise in class: in-class work, P33, may.
units.anchor: Integrate work toward assessments into class meetings and other planned interactions
units.fit_note: In-class work embedded in the course, not necessarily proctored.

units.why: Strategy: 'Ground assessments in the unique context of the course and draw from embedded, real-world scenarios' rather than generic tasks: P35, may.
units.anchor: Ground assessments in the unique context of the course

units.why: Strategy: 'Incorporate opportunities to receive feedback on learning and performance via drafts and revisions': P35, may.
units.anchor: Incorporate opportunities to receive feedback on learning and performance via drafts

units.why: Strategy: 'Ask students to contribute original insights, analyses and other perspectives': P35, may.
units.anchor: Ask students to contribute original insights, analyses and other perspectives

units.why: Strategy: 'Include moments when students need to be conversant about the content, nature and progress of their own work': students explain their work, P34, may.
units.anchor: Include moments when students need to be conversant about the content, nature and progress

units.why: Strategy: 'Ask students to express their learning in different genres, formats and modalities': P35, may.
units.anchor: Ask students to express their learning in different genres, formats and modalities

units.why: Strategy: 'Examine assignments for their validity to what they’re attempting to assess': P35, may.
units.anchor: Examine assignments for their validity to what they’re attempting to assess

units.why: 'None of these strategies are foolproof ways to ensure that generative AI is not used in inappropriate ways': AI misuse cannot be fully prevented, P82, informs.
units.anchor: None of these strategies are foolproof ways to ensure that generative AI is not used

units.why: If an instructor integrates AI 'it is important that all students are supported in the use of digital technologies rather than relying on extant, uneven literacies': equitable preparation, P51, should.
units.anchor: it is important that all students are supported in the use of digital technologies
units.fit_note: Equity in preparation and support, not cost or access to tools.

units.why: Suggests 'walking students through the process of using AI for a particular task, providing tips for effective use': advice on effective use of AI, P93, may.
units.anchor: for a particular task, providing tips for effective use of AI for that task
units.fit_note: Instructor support for students using AI, including tips and tutorials; partly P70/P72.

units.why: AI 'has shown potential to be effective for learning when used in an assistive capacity while brainstorming or discovering ideas and approaches': P15, may.
units.anchor: Brainstorming or discovering ideas and approaches
units.fit_note: Framed as potential effective uses, not a permission.

units.why: Lists 'summarizing, synthesizing or transforming information and other content' as an effective use: a study-aid use, P14, may.
units.anchor: Summarizing, synthesizing or transforming information and other content
units.fit_note: Framed as potential effective uses, not a permission.

units.why: Lists 'interpreting, analyzing and strategizing with data' as an effective use: P89, may.
units.anchor: Interpreting, analyzing and strategizing with data
units.fit_note: Framed as potential effective uses, not a permission.

units.why: Lists 'giving formative feedback on ideas, drafts or other material' as an effective use: nearest P91 (writing support), may.
units.anchor: Giving formative feedback on ideas, drafts or other material
units.fit_note: Feedback on drafts rather than proofreading; framed as potential effective uses.

units.why: Lists 'coaching, tutoring or supporting students' learning, studying and practice in the course' as an effective use: tutor role, P12, may.
units.anchor: Coaching, tutoring or supporting students’ learning, studying and practice in the course
units.fit_note: Framed as potential effective uses, not a permission.

units.why: Lists 'offering different or divergent possibilities for approaches to a task' as an effective use: exploring approaches, P15, may.
units.anchor: Offering different or divergent possibilities for approaches to a task
units.fit_note: Framed as potential effective uses, not a permission.

units.why: 'Students should review all AI output for accuracy, appropriateness and quality': a verification duty, P31, should.
units.anchor: students should review all AI output for accuracy, appropriateness and quality

units.why: Students should 'understand that the output represents only one possibility for understanding and responding to an issue among many': keeps students as thinkers, P32, should.
units.anchor: the output represents only one possibility for understanding and responding to an issue

units.why: 'In many cases, it will be important for students to document their use of generative AI': disclosure expectation, P24, should.
units.anchor: it will be important for students to document their use of generative AI

units.why: Documentation may be 'a more detailed explanation of tools, tasks and outcomes that highlights the student’s agency and decision-making process (similar to a methods section)': content of disclosure, P26, informs.
units.anchor: a more detailed explanation of tools, tasks and outcomes that highlights the student’s agency
units.fit_note: Reflective explanation of tools, tasks and outcomes; not full transcripts.

units.why: Says instructors 'may use generative AI tools to enhance their efforts to support student learning and success': what instructors may do, P59, may.
units.anchor: Instructors may use generative AI tools to enhance their efforts to support student learning and

units.why: Lists 'designing or getting feedback on instructional artifacts such as handouts, rubrics, lesson plans' as effective instructor uses: P59, may.
units.anchor: Designing or getting feedback on instructional artifacts such as handouts, rubrics, lesson plans

units.why: Lists 'implementing AI-driven course assistants, tutors or support agents' as an effective instructor use: a course-specific tool, P17, may.
units.anchor: Implementing AI-driven course assistants, tutors or support agents
units.fit_note: Instructors may deploy course AI assistants; nothing says students are limited to them.

units.why: Lists 'composing effective feedback on student work' as an effective instructor use: AI-drafted feedback, P101, may.
units.anchor: Composing effective feedback on student work
units.fit_note: Permits AI to compose feedback; conditions come from the separate duty to review output.

units.why: Lists 'generating a variety of questions, prompts, scenarios and tasks for students to engage' as an effective instructor use: P59, may.
units.anchor: Generating a variety of questions, prompts, scenarios and tasks for students to engage

units.why: 'Similar to students, instructors should review all AI output for accuracy, appropriateness and quality': verification duty for instructors, P31, should.
units.anchor: instructors should review all AI output for accuracy, appropriateness and quality

units.why: 'A recommended practice for instructors is maintaining transparency around how they are using generative AI in ways that align with expectations for students': instructor disclosure, P47, should.
units.anchor: maintaining transparency around how they are using generative AI

units.why: 'Instructors should not use generative AI in place of their own judgment to determine numerical or letter grades': humans assign grades, P46, should-not.
units.anchor: use generative AI in place of their own judgment to determine numerical or letter grades

units.why: The footnote says the grading recommendation does not apply to approved grading platforms or 'automated scoring of closed-ended questions': conditions for AI-assisted grading, P101, informs.
units.anchor: does not apply to software or digital platforms that have been approved for use in

units.why: 'Student work and other intellectual property should not be shared with third-party AI tools without student permission': protects student work, P49, should-not; binds instructors.
units.anchor: student work and other intellectual property should not be shared with third-party AI tools
units.fit_note: Binds instructors sharing student work, not students uploading course materials.

units.why: Instructors 'are encouraged to work with CELT' for support with 'developing generative AI literacies and skills': faculty support, P63, should.
units.anchor: instructors are encouraged to work with the UK Center for the Enhancement of Learning and

units.why: Invites the community to 'contact UKADVANCE@uky.edu with questions, ideas and recommendations as well as feedback': inviting feedback, P54, may.
units.anchor: Contact UKADVANCE@uky.edu with questions, ideas and recommendations as well as feedback

units.why: The curated list offers resources 'for instructors and students who are eager to learn more about how generative AI works': learning resources, P70, informs.
units.anchor: UK ADVANCE offers the following short list of curated resources as a starting place
units.fit_note: Curated reading list, not training or curricular literacy.

units.why: Lists 'authoritative frameworks and explanations for AI literacy in education' (MLA-CCCC, EDUCAUSE, UNESCO): pointers to literacy resources, P70, informs.
units.anchor: Authoritative frameworks and explanations for AI literacy in education include
units.fit_note: Pointers to external frameworks, not offered training.
